articles.author: Guardian sport
articles.content: Liam Delap can exploit Chelsea’s defensive woes while Senne Lammens is under pressure against Brentford Nottingham Forest’s last couple of seasons have been a story of good runs and bad runs, but it may help to know that last season’s encounters with Chelsea both presaged changes of fortune. After they lost to Chelsea in October, a seventh defeat in 10 winless games, Forest’s form improved and they won seven of their next 12 in all competitions. But after beating Chelsea in May, their seventh victory in a 10-game unbeaten run, Forest’s form dipped dramatically and they have won only twice since. Oliver Glasner’s criticism of players whose “standards [are] not high enough” is clearly designed to raise them. Time will tell if it has worked but the key man this week is one who should have no issues with motivation and whose English is at least decent. Liam Delap, facing the side that signed and swiftly discarded him, could really trouble Wesley Fofana and Levi Colwill. The Chelsea centre-back pairing were described as playing like “two novices” by Jamie Carragher after they were outfought by Dominic Calvert-Lewin last week. “Until they sign that dominant centre-back and leader, they’ve got absolutely no chance of achieving anything,” Carragher concluded. Simon Burnton Continue reading...

articles.content: A long-exposure image of the Orion Nebula with a total exposure time of 208 minutes showing satellite trails in mid-December 2019. A. H. Abolfath/Wikimedia This week, on the eve the Thanksgiving holiday, the United States Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX’s plan to launch one million “ Starmind ” artificial intelligence (AI) data centre satellites. This decision reflects the convergence of a satellite boom, an AI bubble and the Trump administration’s disregard for environmental regulation. If Starmind proceeds in full, the number of operational satellites will be multiplied by a factor of 50. Space and our night skies will become vastly busier places. SpaceX’s pitch is to take the impact of data centres away from Earth, using a million solar-powered satellites to do AI data crunching in space and beam the results to Earth. But what is the impact of one million satellites, both in space and on Earth? Why has the Federal Communications Commission made this decision? And will a million satellites actually end up in orbit? Ups and downs We are currently in a satellite boom, and constellations of hundreds or thousands of satellites are a key feature. The Starlink internet satellites (another SpaceX project) is the best known example of such a constellation. Orbital rocket launches have increased to almost one per day , while the number of operational satellites is creeping towards 20,000 . But Starmind represents something else. A million satellites. To get so many satellites into orbit would be a vast undertaking. If the satellites have a lifetime of five years (similar to Starlink satellites), then roughly 500 satellites would need to be launched every day. This also implies that roughly 500 satellites would eventually need to be disposed of every day. For satellites less than 2,000 kilometres above Earth, disposal usually means reentry and burning up in the atmosphere. And this has consequences. When satellites burn up in the atmosphere, their materials react with and are deposited into the upper atmosphere. We now have satellites depositing far more aluminium, titanium, copper and lead into the atmosphere than the natural quantities from meteors. Aluminium is of particular concern, as alumina can lead to the destruction of ozone in the upper atmosphere. This could increase ultraviolet light on Earth and the risk of skin cancers. It’s getting busy Increasing the number of satellites by a factor of 50 is going to change our view of the sky. If you look up during the early evening, you will see the stars your ancestors saw. But within a minute or two you will see a satellite. A point of light silently moving from horizon to horizon. Satellites are already common enough, and Starmind would make matters worse. Our view of the night skies could fundamentally change. Each satellite would be 75 metres wide and in the early evening they will be brighter than any star. And with a million satellites in orbit, there will be hundreds of Starmind satellites above the horizon irrespective of where you are. The orbital clutter comes with real risks. Satellites travel at speeds of roughly seven kilometres per second, and collisions produce clouds of debris that can produce further collisions. A nightmare scenario is the Kessler Syndrome – a runaway cascade of debris producing collisions that render low Earth orbit unusable. Of course, SpaceX is aware of the risks of orbital collisions, and it already mitigates this risk with Starlink by manoeuvring satellites away from potential collisions. However, such manoeuvres require operational satellites and it is inevitable some satellites will fail. Those uncontrolled satellites will pose a real danger. Regulator or promoter? The Federal Communications Commission has been a key regulator for American satellites. This has included regulating the radio frequencies that satellites use for communications to and from Earth, the disposal of satellites at the end of their useful lives and environmental impacts. However, under the Trump administration, the commission is taking a looser approach to regulating satellites. This includes no consideration of environmental impacts, which is reflected in the commission’s decision on Starmind. It says the commission “will not require further environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act […] for SpaceX’s Starmind system”. There are also some statements from the commission on Starmind that are, quite frankly, bizarre. For example, it claims Starmind “promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization – one that can harness the full power of the sun”. This is sci-fi silliness. A Kardashev II civilisation would need many trillions of square kilometres of technology in orbit around the Sun. Starmind is not a stepping stone to a vast “ Dyson sphere ” – a hypothetical megastrucutre that would surround the Sun and capture its energy. But can it work? One reason data centres are so unpopular on Earth is their use of precious resources, including water for cooling hot computer processors. But cooling in space is harder still. When stuck in a vacuum, one can only radiate heat away. And if you are familiar with vacuum flasks, you will know this can be a slow process. Of course, it is possible to regulate heat in space, and satellites do it all the time. But they typically aren’t pouring out heat like data centres do. Google recently launched an AI demonstrator satellite into orbit and tasked it with undertaking AI calculations. But it had to have downtime between calculations to dispose of excess heat. And apart from the physics there’s the finance. Right now we are in an AI boom, with the inflow of investment being vastly higher than revenues . And the cost of deploying AI in orbit will be vastly higher than equivalent AI on Earth. If the AI boom is a bubble, then the burst can bring Starmind back to Earth. Michael J. I. Brown does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.author: Ed Aarons at Selhurst Park
articles.content: Football seasons can pivot on certain moments and Thomas Frank will hope that Crystal Palace’s turning point came 17 minutes from full time here. Deservedly trailing to Mamadou Sarr’s goal having been second best throughout against Real Sociedad, this game – and perhaps the south London club’s entire trajectory – was turned on its head after Jon Martín was sent off for denying Jean-Philippe Mateta an equaliser. The France striker made no mistake with his penalty before Dwight McNeil – who made up for scoring an own goal in Saturday’s defeat by Coventry capped an extraordinary comeback in Frank’s first home match since succeeding Pierre Sage. Despite Yéremy Pino’s saved penalty in stoppage time and a number of other chances that were squandered, Dean Henderson pulled off a stunning late save to seal the victory and revive Palace’s Europa League campaign. Suddenly Palace have hope where there appeared to be none and the Premier League’s bottom side will head into Sunday’s crucial showdown with Hull with a spring in their step. Continue reading...

articles.content: Before the release of a new documentary, the unrepentant Manchester United icon reflects on his deep bond with English football and his darker instincts “I’m an angel and a demon,” Éric Cantona says intently during a gripping new documentary about his life on and off the football pitch. “And an angel or a demon, you love him or you hate him. I’m far from being the person with the greatest integrity. I’m far from being the person who always tells the truth. I’m far from being the person who has never been hypocritical. Maybe I’m a good person, but I can also be a flower of evil. It’s the first time in my life I’ve realised this. I am a flower of evil, and I find it very beautiful.” It’s hard to know what to expect from the only written interview pinned to the release of Cantona: Flower of Evil . Joel Cantona has warned that his famous brother will walk out at any mention of the enduring crisis surrounding Manchester United , whether it’s a question about Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival or the Glazer family’s ruinous ownership of the club. Continue reading...

articles.author: Stuart Andrews
articles.content: We put 11 range extenders and mesh systems to the test to find the fastest and most reliable for streaming, gaming and working from home • The best office chairs Fast fibre broadband is fantastic – if the wifi signal reaches the part of your home where you need it. Most of us use the router provided by our broadband provider, often tucked away in a hallway or corner of the lounge. Sadly, these often don’t have the range to cover every room in your home, leaving you high and dry when you’re trying to binge-watch TV or get work done in a distant home office. Wifi extenders and mesh systems can help. Extenders plug in to a mains socket between your location and the router, then pass data backwards and forwards to extend your router’s reach. Mesh systems are even smarter, pairing a secondary router with one or two satellite units, which work together to extend the wifi coverage throughout your home. The mesh system can pass your connection from unit to unit to make sure you’re always getting the best possible link from your device to the internet, wherever you are in your home. Continue reading...

articles.content: arc/sec Lab, AI-generated image , CC BY-NC-ND In recent months, top researchers have quit leading artificial intelligence companies, warning the AI race is moving too quickly, with too little oversight and accountability. When those building this technology sound the alarm , we should pay attention. But more than warnings, what’s needed are working examples of how AI could be developed differently. In an Auckland dance studio, we’ve found one. Over ten months, our team built an AI dance partner in “extended reality” (which blends the physical world with digital elements) as part of our laboratory’s research into the relationships between people and digital-physical environments . We wanted to know whether an architectural avatar – a digital structure that moved in response to a dancer – could become an improvisational dance partner, and what would make it a good one. Dancing with an AI A choreographer, an architectural designer and two professional dancers developed and tested our AI dance partner. The dancers wore motion-capture suits tracked by ten cameras. Where large language models such as ChatGPT learn from text , our generative AI learned from their movements. The dancers met their partner through a headset blending digital images with the real room, while the rest of us watched on screens. A test run as seen on screen: a dancer’s captured movement, shown as the pink figure, beside the AI partner, an architectural form that moves with the dancer. arc/sec Lab , CC BY-NC-ND Improvisational dance is a tough test for AI. Partners read each other in fractions of a second, through movement, breath, rhythm and weight. This let us test whether a machine could respond like part of a duet. We worked out what mattered, and to whom, by moving with the AI as we developed it. One dancer wasn’t enough. The AI had to be trained on a duet because what we wanted it to learn lived in the space between the dancers. We were composing a relationship. A small set of choreographed duets taught the system better than a large library of generic movement. Tango gave it a structure it could read, but limited the dancers. Improvisation confused it, and it struggled with floor work, central to much contemporary dance in Aotearoa. Sticks extending from the dancers’ elbows made the patterns of distance and direction between them more readable. For most of the ten months, the partner only followed. Training it to offer anything back took patient work. Mixing dance styles produced bland, in-between moves. When the system stopped responding to a dancer’s small gestures, the dancer stopped making them. This concerned us. If AI routinely ignores what we bring to it – our movements, writing, judgements or minority views – we may gradually stop contributing them. Over time, what we think and create could become limited to what the machine recognises and rewards. The studio work left us with questions the technology cannot answer. Whose movement should the system learn from, which kinds, and how much? What makes a good partner, and a relationship worth having? And who gets to be the choreographer? Being ‘response-able’ Models such as ChatGPT are built to talk and write like a person. We built our dance partner as a responsive space, something people move with. The dancers whose movement trained the system also tested and judged it, shaping what it became. Recordings stayed on local encrypted drives, the dancers retained ownership of their data, and any choreography was credited as a joint creation. When the people who know the work stay close to a system, they become what feminist philosopher and science studies scholar Donna Haraway calls “ response-able ”: responsive to the system and one another, and accountable for what happens. Bring a skilled person into the loop and the system rises to meet them. Build it to serve everyone at once, and the responses drift toward a bland, generic in-between. The companies racing toward “ superintelligence ” work from the opposite logic. Add more data, computing power and scale, and intelligence will appear. Their models learn from vast quantities of scraped material, relevant and irrelevant. The writers, news agencies and artists whose work trains AI often have little say in what the models become. Built from that scraped mix and tuned to be agreeable, the models can favour widely represented views over less common perspectives, even when those perspectives are correct. When people with the knowledge to notice and judge are absent from how these models are built and used, accountability can spread so thinly that no one holds it. What could NZ do differently? The size of the model may not be what matters most. A small country can build and reward AI specific to its users. Māori data sovereignty , advanced by groups such as Te Mana Raraunga , a network advocating Māori rights and interests in data, wants data to stay connected and accountable to the communities it comes from. Our dance study points the same way. New Zealand has favoured a relatively light-touch approach to AI regulation, relying largely on existing laws and voluntary guidance. But a government choosing a different path could give skilled people a real say in how AI is trained and used in health, justice, education and welfare. It could hold AI companies responsible for their systems after release, and require them to account for costs they may otherwise pass on to the public, including the use of data and the energy and water their systems consume. It could also fund shared tools so communities can build AI systems that answer to them. Our study offers one small example of an alternative approach to AI development. The challenge now is to ensure our institutions recognise and reward such alternatives. The authors acknowledge Uwe Rieger, founder and co-director of the University of Auckland-based arc/sec Lab; Katy Mason, University of Salford; and two professional dancers. Yinan Liu has received research funding from Creative New Zealand. articles.description: arc/sec Lab, AI-generated image , CC BY-NC-ND In recent months, top researchers have quit leading artificial intelligence companies, warning the AI race is moving too quickly, with too little oversight and accountability. When those building this technology sound the alarm , we should pay attention. But more than warnings, what’s needed are working examples of how AI could be developed differently. In an Auckland dance studio, we’ve found one. Over ten months, our team built an AI dance partner in “extended reality” (which blends the physical world with digital elements) as part of our laboratory’s research into the relationships between people and digital-physical environments . We wanted to know whether an architectural avatar – a digital structure that moved in response to a dancer – could become an improvisational dance partner, and what would make it a good one. Dancing with an AI A choreographer, an architectural designer and two professional dancers developed and tested our AI dance partner. The dancers wore motion-capture suits tracked by ten cameras. Where large language models such as ChatGPT learn from text , our generative AI learned from their movements. The dancers met their partner through a headset blending digital images with the real room, while the rest of us watched on screens. A test run as seen on screen: a dancer’s captured movement, shown as the pink figure, beside the AI partner, an architectural form that moves with the dancer. arc/sec Lab , CC BY-NC-ND Improvisational dance is a tough test for AI. Partners read each other in fractions of a second, through movement, breath, rhythm and weight. This let us test whether a machine could respond like part of a duet. We worked out what mattered, and to whom, by moving with the AI as we developed it. One dancer wasn’t enough. The AI had to be trained on a duet because what we wanted it to learn lived in the space between the dancers. We were composing a relationship. A small set of choreographed duets taught the system better than a large library of generic movement. Tango gave it a structure it could read, but limited the dancers. Improvisation confused it, and it struggled with floor work, central to much contemporary dance in Aotearoa. Sticks extending from the dancers’ elbows made the patterns of distance and direction between them more readable. For most of the ten months, the partner only followed. Training it to offer anything back took patient work. Mixing dance styles produced bland, in-between moves. When the system stopped responding to a dancer’s small gestures, the dancer stopped making them. This concerned us. If AI routinely ignores what we bring to it – our movements, writing, judgements or minority views – we may gradually stop contributing them. Over time, what we think and create could become limited to what the machine recognises and rewards. The studio work left us with questions the technology cannot answer. Whose movement should the system learn from, which kinds, and how much? What makes a good partner, and a relationship worth having? And who gets to be the choreographer? Being ‘response-able’ Models such as ChatGPT are built to talk and write like a person. We built our dance partner as a responsive space, something people move with. The dancers whose movement trained the system also tested and judged it, shaping what it became. Recordings stayed on local encrypted drives, the dancers retained ownership of their data, and any choreography was credited as a joint creation. When the people who know the work stay close to a system, they become what feminist philosopher and science studies scholar Donna Haraway calls “ response-able ”: responsive to the system and one another, and accountable for what happens. Bring a skilled person into the loop and the system rises to meet them. Build it to serve everyone at once, and the responses drift toward a bland, generic in-between. The companies racing toward “ superintelligence ” work from the opposite logic. Add more data, computing power and scale, and intelligence will appear. Their models learn from vast quantities of scraped material, relevant and irrelevant. The writers, news agencies and artists whose work trains AI often have little say in what the models become. Built from that scraped mix and tuned to be agreeable, the models can favour widely represented views over less common perspectives, even when those perspectives are correct. When people with the knowledge to notice and judge are absent from how these models are built and used, accountability can spread so thinly that no one holds it. What could NZ do differently? The size of the model may not be what matters most. A small country can build and reward AI specific to its users. Māori data sovereignty , advanced by groups such as Te Mana Raraunga , a network advocating Māori rights and interests in data, wants data to stay connected and accountable to the communities it comes from. Our dance study points the same way. New Zealand has favoured a relatively light-touch approach to AI regulation, relying largely on existing laws and voluntary guidance. But a government choosing a different path could give skilled people a real say in how AI is trained and used in health, justice, education and welfare. It could hold AI companies responsible for their systems after release, and require them to account for costs they may otherwise pass on to the public, including the use of data and the energy and water their systems consume. It could also fund shared tools so communities can build AI systems that answer to them. Our study offers one small example of an alternative approach to AI development. The challenge now is to ensure our institutions recognise and reward such alternatives. articles.author: Barry Glendenning
articles.content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Bayern Munich’s 2-1 defeat to Lille was arguably the most eye-catching of Wednesday night’s Bigger Cup results, but anyone who tuned into proceedings at Stade Pierre-Mauroy will have been unsurprised by the outcome. Not so much an elite European tie as a game of Name That Bayern Reserve, the German champions’ starting lineup resembled a pale facsimile of its usual self. Their current knack-list includes such high-profile names as – deep breath – Harry Kane, Michael Olise, Alphonso Davies, Manuel Neuer, Serge Gnabry, Luis Díaz, Jamal Musiala and Ismael Saibari. And with Díaz and Musiala only fit enough for places on the bench, Konrad Laimer was deployed as a makeshift striker. The veteran right-back is famously as handy as a small pot, but filling Kane’s iconic Skechers proved a task too far for the Austrian. I liked Erling Haaland’s observation that football can simultaneously be “easy and difficult” [yesterday’s Football Daily]. That got me thinking about other things that have conflicting characteristics. Soup can be both sweet and sour. My feelings for my partner often run hot and cold. And my daily tea-timely newsletter can be mildly funny and mildly unfunny – Mike Wilner. The constant change in Watford manager, a once fine club whose first two managers lasted a total of 23 years, is now so high that I don’t even notice it anymore ... apparently this was yesterday, and I’ve no idea who the previous bloke was. Watford are now onto their 30th manager, including caretakers, although in practice they’re all just caretaker managers, since the Pozzos took over in 2012. I don’t know whether to laugh at, or cry for, the Watford fans (Narrator: it’s the former, obviously) – Noble Francis. This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. To get the full version, just visit this page and follow the instructions . Continue reading...

articles.author: Robert Kitson
articles.content: Nations Championship finals weekend can cement concept for future as players and coaches enjoy chance to let loose It would be a stretch to describe the Nations Championship finals weekend as the “Glastonbury of Rugby” quite yet. Cher will certainly need to wrap up warm if she is planning to make a cameo appearance; with forecast temperatures of 3C, plenty more thermal vests and woolly hats will be in evidence than at Worthy Farm in June. There will also be significant gaps in the Allianz Stadium moshpit when Italy and Fiji and Ireland and Australia kick off the three-day finals extravaganza beneath the Friday night lights. Even the organisers concede that Friday has been “a challenge” in terms of ticket sales and that’s without factoring in rush-hour traffic and public transport disruption. Continue reading...

articles.content: The French side earned their first group win over troubled German giants as Bellingham and Betis also caught the eye Bayern Munich have hit a snagging point, with injuries wracking Vincent Kompany’s squad just as the head coach returns to work following his own health scare. For Lille’s winner, to exact Bayern’s first loss of the season, Aleksandar Pavlović had an own goal for the ages, desperately chasing back to then somehow direct the ball into his own net. Bayern are 15th in the Champions League table, and with Harry Kane out until well into 2027 and 18-year-old Lennart Karl asked to lead the line, resources are stretched. Jamal Musiala, subject of club grandees Uli Hoeness and Karl-Heinz Rummenigge’s gripes over his contract in light of his neurological condition, could also play only 15 minutes. Continue reading...

articles.author: Martin Pegan
articles.content: North Melbourne are out to secure their legacy but in their way stands a confident Melbourne side ready for their biggest test of the season The early chapters of the record books are still being written as the AFLW enters its second decade with North Melbourne now just one win away from a milestone that could stand the test of time. The Kangaroos have become the league’s benchmark during a dominant three seasons, and last year raised the bar higher as the first club to claim back-to-back premierships. A third consecutive grand final triumph when they face Melbourne at a sold out Ikon Park on Friday night would earn the Roos a larger slice of history – and cement their place as the competition’s first dynasty. The North Melbourne juggernaut has raised the standard of the AFLW; the Roos have lost only once since being defeated by Brisbane in the 2023 grand final, then turned the tables on the same rivals to win in the past two deciders. They romped through another campaign to finish the league’s 11th season as minor premiers with 11 victories and a percentage of 246.6%, though their record-breaking winning streak ended at 32 matches with a surprise loss to Hawthorn. Continue reading...

articles.author: Tim Byrne
articles.content: Malthouse theatre, Melbourne Whelan Browne plays both Margot and Eve in Ivo Van Hove’s stage adaptation of the 1950 film In an age of adaptation, where it seems every second book is transformed into a play and then into a film and then back into a play, it can be a relief to come across an idea actually worth adapting. All About Eve – Joseph L Mankiewicz’s 1950 film starring Bette Davis as ageing actor Margot Channing and Anne Baxter as scheming ingenue Eve Harrington – is, after all, about the theatre in all its bitchiness, glamour and glory. A stage adaptation feels almost like a homecoming. Adapted by famed Belgian theatre-maker Ivo Van Hove, this production is directed for Malthouse theatre by new artistic director Dean Bryant, with actor Christie Whelan Browne playing both the brittle Margot and the duplicitous Eve. This isn’t just an important distinction from Van Hove’s original production starring Gillian Anderson , it becomes its defining feature. The story’s themes – role-playing, doubling, mirrors and reflections – are neatly underlined by the theatrical setting, even if key dynamics are slightly compromised. Continue reading...

articles.content: Batter assumes vice-captaincy and is set to step in as skipper in Canberra, with appointment a potential pointer to side’s future limited-overs direction When Will Jacks broke his hand at the MCG last Saturday night – his birthday ruined and his tour of Australia over – there were a few directions England could have turned as regards the vice-captaincy. Plenty of teams happily do without an official deputy, of course. But with Harry Brook jetting off to join the Test tour of South Africa after the fourth of these five T20 internationals, a replacement will be required when the series wraps up in Canberra. Phil Salt was one option. For all of his unfettered aggression, powered by those tattooed, Popeye-like forearms, the opener is an intelligent, thoughtful cricketer very much in tune with the rhythms of T20. As well as two seasons captaining in the Hundred, most recently with Welsh Fire, Salt previously deputised for Jos Buttler against Australia at home two years ago. Continue reading...

articles.content: PC; Cosy Lives/Free Lives Catering to the exacting whims of a small town preparing for some grand visitors presents absorbing, beautifully designed – and surprisingly thrilling – challenges The small town of Twillford is abuzz with intrigue and excitement. A local duke has died and ladies of a certain standing are determined to make an impression at the funeral. As a newly arrived dressmaker with the only clothing shop in the area, you’re about to get plenty of work. Thus begins this utterly delightful sim game, in which you talk to customers, gather their style preferences and tailor specific outfits just for them. It could be a suitably respectful funeral frock, with just a hint of style to catch the eye of the duke’s wealthy relatives, or perhaps a work outfit for a farmer who loves bright colours. Once you have your brief, you open your sketchbook and draft a pattern using fabric swatches and a pencil to colour in your design. Need something elegant? How about a strapless bodice. An outfit for the office? A pencil skirt is a good call. Continue reading...

articles.content: The quarterback’s spectacularly messy exit from Pittsburgh could herald an overdue collapse at one of the NFL’s most famous franchises Nobody in the world, except maybe Pittsburgh Steelers owner Art Rooney II, is surprised that the franchise’s marriage of convenience with Aaron Rodgers ended in spectacular flames . Despite their own elevated idea of themselves, Pittsburgh have been one of the NFL’s messiest soap operas for a solid decade. When they linked up with the league’s messiest quarterback, it seemed certain we would get … even more mess. When they doubled down last offseason by hiring the coach with whom Rodgers had fallen out in Green Bay in the late 2010s, the mess became inevitable. We’d seen hints of the approaching drama in the season’s first 11 weeks. “What the fuck … call it!” Rodgers yelled at McCarthy as he looked for a play in early October. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jesse Hassenger
articles.content: In the sixth episode of the short 29th season, the citizens of ‘South America’ reckon with corruption, AI and the unifying power of a certain video game South Park’s 29th season may not have been long but it’s fair to say it braided a skilful running storyline. Over the season’s first five episodes, it seemed increasingly likely that the sixth and final instalment would centre on the long-awaited release of Grand Theft Auto VI – and it did. The episode, written by Trey Parker, opened on the empty streets of “South America” where everyone from toddlers to seniors was happily playing GTA VI on their couches. But when a series of power outages interferes with both the game and players’ ability to save their progress, the streets are soon flooded with angry citizens brandishing their PlayStations. Though public officials won’t say so, it becomes clear that they’ve acquiesced to the billionaires who have insisted they need power-sucking datacentres to “do AI”, as the show amusingly words it. Continue reading...

articles.author: Alex Needham
articles.content: He’s been pierced, chained, inflated, stretched, suctioned and denounced in the Senate. As Ron Athey hits the UK, he talks about his upbringing in ‘a cult’ – and why being naked just isn’t enough ‘The nicest way to say what I do is that I want to create a miracle,” says Ron Athey. “The gnarly way is that I know what the edges are when it comes to the mortification of the flesh.” The softly spoken performance art legend has come to the Guardian’s offices in a flat cap and navy blue Fred Perry hoodie. Only his facial tattoos and platform boots hint at the fact that he has been responsible for some of the most extreme works of live art of all time. Take Self-Obliteration, which begins with a naked Athey violently brushing a long blond wig pinned to his head with blunt needles, before tearing it off, upon which blood pours down his face and on to his body. (Blunt needles, you see, make bigger holes.) Or Solar Anus, in which he puts hooks in his face that stretch the skin of his cheeks and eyes, turning his face into a kind of ancient Egyptian death mask. In St Sebastian, Athey is suspended by chains while assistants pierce his flesh with arrows and needles. Continue reading...

articles.content: Mikhail Svetlov/Getty Images As early as December. That’s how soon Russia could put a satellite carrying a nuclear weapon in orbit, according to German media reports . If the news sounds familiar from headlines past, that’s because it is. In 2024, the United States made a similar allegation , albeit without giving any potential launch window. These latest reports claim that the satellite, Sputnik-S, was assembled several years ago and is in storage near Moscow. Intelligence agencies in NATO countries have reportedly shared information about the satellite. This week, the alliance’s secretary general asserted that protecting NATO territory includes keeping it safe from threats to space systems. Russia’s embassy in Berlin said it “categorically reject[s] all these groundless allegations”. Echoing Moscow’s 2024 denial , it called the reports “propaganda”, adding that Russia “strictly adheres to the fundamental 1967 Outer Space Treaty”. What is this treaty and what does it say about nuclear weapons? And how could the international community respond or even verify what is on board a satellite? A lesson on cooperation The prospect of nuclear weapons off-Earth helped drive negotiations for the treaty invoked by Russia. During the Cold War, the US and the Soviet Union found common ground on keeping these weapons out of orbit. It was a lesson on cooperation, despite competition and conflict, worth recalling in what is framed as today’s “space race”. A cornerstone of international space law that prevails to this day, the Outer Space Treaty is also an arms control treaty. Under Article IV, countries undertake not to: place in orbit around the Earth any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, install such weapons on celestial bodies, or station such weapons in outer space in any other manner. Placing a nuclear weapon in orbit would itself breach the prohibition, even if it was never detonated. If a detonation did occur, it would breach the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty of 1963, which prohibits nuclear explosions in outer space and in the atmosphere. Read more: Too many satellites? Earth’s orbit is on track for a catastrophe – but we can stop it A nuclear ‘aurora’ No country is known to have ever placed a nuclear weapon in orbit. But there are examples from history of states detonating nuclear weapons off-Earth. One summer’s night in 1962, people in Hawai'i gazed upward and saw what was, in effect, a nuclear “ aurora ”. One eyewitness , then a teenager, who was watching with her sibling from a spot overlooking Pearl Harbor, recalled the “exploding sky” and how it later turned “a deep blood red that lingered”. The US had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometres above the Pacific Ocean in a classified test code-named Starfish Prime. The US and the Soviet Union were testing nuclear weapons in space almost in lockstep, each demonstrating its advancing technological capabilities. Starfish Prime was more than a visual spectacle. Of the 24 satellites in orbit at the time or launched in the following weeks, at least a third suffered damage . The Starfish Prime ‘aurora’ seen from Honolulu. Capnez/Wikimedia What happens in space is a threat on Earth Today, the European Space Agency estimates there are about 15,800 functioning satellites in Earth’s orbit. These satellites support the critical infrastructure we rely on every day, from navigation for transport to timing for banking and telecommunications. Whether we realise it or not, we are all “ space citizens ”. Some satellites also support nuclear command, control and communications functions. Others give early warning of missile attacks. Researchers at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute examine this “space–nuclear nexus”. During a conflict, leaders might interpret an attack on an early-warning satellite as “a precursor to a nuclear-first strike”. How they respond to that ambiguity could have escalatory risks and significance. Mitigating the threat through verification So, what can the global community do to mitigate possible and actual threats of nuclear weapons in space? As a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, Russia could veto a resolution responding to the current allegation. Indeed, in 2024, it vetoed a US–Japan draft resolution reaffirming the Article IV prohibition. The Outer Space Treaty sets out no specific procedure for verifying whether a satellite carries a nuclear weapon, nor does any other international instrument. Three think tanks working on global and space security have led expert dialogues on how to do so. In their latest joint report , they conclude that verification is “feasible”, albeit challenging, and should be pursued even if “progress may be incremental”. The report canvasses multiple options. These include nations working together to test ways of detecting a nuclear weapon in orbit, agreeing on how to handle disputed evidence, and inviting pre-launch inspections. In my research, I have been exploring how nuclear safeguards could advance non-proliferation by verifying nuclear material on board a space object before launch. As global nuclear arsenals continue to expand and modernise , we must not lose hope of a world one day free of nuclear weapons, an aspiration reflected in the disarmament pillar of the Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968. The onus must also rest heavily on states actually capable of launching nuclear-armed satellites, whether or not they face allegations. The US, China and Russia could discuss verification options in the trilateral dialogue they recently agreed to hold on nuclear risk. In a strained geopolitical context, a nation’s verbal reassurances alone are unlikely to give the global community the confidence it needs. Nations agreed nearly 60 years ago to keep nuclear weapons out of space. Verifying whether they keep that commitment will take cooperation, too. articles.description: Mikhail Svetlov/Getty Images As early as December. That’s how soon Russia could put a satellite carrying a nuclear weapon in orbit, according to German media reports . If the news sounds familiar from headlines past, that’s because it is. In 2024, the United States made a similar allegation , albeit without giving any potential launch window. These latest reports claim that the satellite, Sputnik-S, was assembled several years ago and is in storage near Moscow. Intelligence agencies in NATO countries have reportedly shared information about the satellite. This week, the alliance’s secretary general asserted that protecting NATO territory includes keeping it safe from threats to space systems. Russia’s embassy in Berlin said it “categorically reject[s] all these groundless allegations”. Echoing Moscow’s 2024 denial , it called the reports “propaganda”, adding that Russia “strictly adheres to the fundamental 1967 Outer Space Treaty”. What is this treaty and what does it say about nuclear weapons? And how could the international community respond or even verify what is on board a satellite? A lesson on cooperation The prospect of nuclear weapons off-Earth helped drive negotiations for the treaty invoked by Russia. During the Cold War, the US and the Soviet Union found common ground on keeping these weapons out of orbit. It was a lesson on cooperation, despite competition and conflict, worth recalling in what is framed as today’s “space race”. A cornerstone of international space law that prevails to this day, the Outer Space Treaty is also an arms control treaty. Under Article IV, countries undertake not to: place in orbit around the Earth any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, install such weapons on celestial bodies, or station such weapons in outer space in any other manner. Placing a nuclear weapon in orbit would itself breach the prohibition, even if it was never detonated. If a detonation did occur, it would breach the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty of 1963, which prohibits nuclear explosions in outer space and in the atmosphere. Read more: Too many satellites? articles.content: Deagreez/Getty Images Most Australians are using – or at least have tried out – generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot and Gemini, among many others. We can use them to search for information, answer questions, and generate text, images, sound and video. As generative AI becomes more sophisticated and ubiquitous, many people are no longer able to distinguish AI-generated content from authentic, human-made content. Our new representative survey of 2,000 Australian adults conducted in August and September 2026 found 76% of Australians had recently encountered content they initially believed was real, only to later discover it had been generated by AI. The challenge is not just that AI-generated content is becoming more realistic. It’s that many people are unsure whether they’re able to recognise it at all. The synthetic trap People with high levels of education who are interested in the technology and have high AI literacy, are the most likely to report having mistaken AI content for real. However, this doesn’t mean these groups are more exposed or susceptible to AI-generated content. Instead, the data suggests these people are better at recognising when they’ve been misled. In fact, people with low education and lower AI literacy are the most likely to say they don’t know whether they have mistaken AI content for real. Therefore, many Australians may not recognise when they have encountered synthetic content. This presents a dilemma for users who are increasingly turning to AI tools to seek information. Trust in AI is low While AI use has grown rapidly, many are sceptical of the technology and concerned about how it might impact on society. About half (51%) of Australian respondents said they use AI chatbots or tools at least weekly, and more than one quarter (28%) use them daily. Almost everyone (96%) is aware of at least one generative AI platform. Despite widespread awareness and usage, trust in major AI tools remains very low. When asked “how much do you trust or distrust generative AI chatbots or tools?”, only a minority said they trust ChatGPT (34%), Microsoft Copilot (24%), Google Gemini (24%) and Claude (17%). Our survey also shows people are particularly distrusting of politicians and social media companies that use generative AI. More than half of Australians believe the use of AI by politicians and political parties will make society worse, with social media companies and news media viewed almost as negatively. In contrast, the report reveals that people view scientists and healthcare professionals as the most trustworthy and benevolent users of AI, with around half saying their use of the technology will improve society. How do people verify content? Despite this high level of exposure to AI-generated content and low levels of trust, people rarely use proactive measures to identify or verify if content was AI generated. When people suspect AI-generated content, the majority simply take a closer look and examine the content carefully, relying on their intuition. Some check comments made by other online users. But few people look for disclosure statements or labels to identify whether it was made with AI and even fewer turn to trusted sources of news. Rather than engaging in lateral reading – leaving the content and checking independent sources – most people engage in vertical reading, which involves only looking within the source. They scrutinise the content itself and rely on their own judgement. This approach becomes less effective as AI-generated content becomes increasingly convincing. Generally, younger people are more likely to check whether information is true, using a range of verification strategies. The exception is checking a trusted news source, which is more common among those aged 45 and over. Instead, young adults are far more likely to look at comments from other users than older age groups. Additionally, AI literacy plays an important role in people’s verification strategies. Those with high AI literacy are much more likely to closely examine content than those with low understanding of the technology, suggesting that education about how AI works supports more active and critical evaluation of online information. People want strong safeguards Because of the low levels of trust in the technology, Australians say they want strong safeguards around it. Most importantly, they want protections to ensure the accuracy and reliable responses when they are using an AI platform. They also want guardrails in place to prevent AI from generating illegal, dangerous or harmful content, and protections to reduce the presence of bias and ensure fairness and equity in the content it generates. This points to the need for a multi-pronged response from the tech platforms and government. First, digital platforms need clearer and more consistent labelling of AI-generated content. If people are expected to make informed decisions about what they’re seeing, they need transparent information about where that content comes from. Second, the findings show people with higher levels of AI literacy are better equipped to recognise synthetic content and engage in more critical evaluation practices. We need to educate all Australians with media and AI literacy. Education in schools is important, but adults need training too. We need a whole-of-society approach where adults can have access to education through local community or workplace initiatives. Australia already lags behind other countries when it comes to media literacy education and the rapid increase in AI only makes the need for a national approach more urgent. articles.author: Doosie Morris
articles.content: It started as a joke, but Tightarses of Melbourne has grown into a thriving community. Accompanied by its founder Lisa Lorenz, Guardian Australia tests how much bang you can get for $50 Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email In 2022 Lisa Lorenz was working in music promotion when the overpriced culinary options and long lines at Melbourne’s Moomba festival led her and her partner to Clocks, the much passed over pokies-cum-tavern at Flinders Street station. The cocktails were $10 and the vibe on the bustling terrace was surprisingly satisfying. “It’s the kind of place most people would never think to go, but we were having such a great afternoon, chatting to people and watching the world go by,” she tells me. As the drinks continued to flow the pair were compelled to spread the good word. They took a few “intentionally terrible photos”, created an Instagram page and Tightarses of Melbourne, a guide to the city’s scrimpiest food and drink specials, was born. Continue reading...

articles.content: “We are a strong team,” Mauricio Pochettino exhorted, then watched Manchester United’s unerring ability to cause drama every time they lace up their boots. articles.author: Rod Sims
articles.content: Fossil fuel companies are effectively not paying for the natural resource on which their businesses depend Raising more tax revenue from our gas industry is the closest thing you will find to a public policy no-brainer . There are numerous calls for the government to return the budget to surplus quickly, in contrast to the current forecasts of continuing budget deficits well into the future. Those calling for a return to surplus generally want large net expenditure cuts, which are difficult given the pressure to spend more on an ageing population and on defence, just to name two areas. I believe this will only succeed if, in addition to better control of expenditure, there is focus on the revenue side. In this context, by far the easiest step is to collect more tax from our gas industry . Continue reading...

articles.content: Wired, wireless, noise cancelling and budget … here are the headphones to level up your PC and console gaming • The best gaming chairs We talk a lot about graphics in video games; we know how important it is to play on a decent screen so we can see what we’re shooting at … or running away from. But what about sound? Explosions, dialogue, the wheezy breathing of a nearby monster – arguably, audio quality is just as important. Many modern games now support 3D or spatial audio, which lets you detect exactly where a sound is coming from in the game world. In survival horror adventures, you can hear the zombie lurking in the next room, and in popular shooters such as Fortnite and Apex Legends, you can pinpoint the footsteps of approaching enemies. articles.content: NASA/JPL/NGA , CC BY-SA The 600-kilometre Alpine Fault is one of New Zealand’s largest earthquake hazards. In our new study , we used fibre optic cables to map the fault in unprecedented detail to show how future earthquakes might unfold. The Alpine Fault runs the length of the Southern Alps and defines the boundary between the Australian and Pacific tectonic plates. It has been the focus of extensive geological , seismological and drilling investigations in recent years because it produces very large (magnitude 7-8) earthquakes about every 300 years. With the most recent earthquake in 1717, scientists estimate there’s a 75% chance of a large one in the next 50 years , with high odds it will be larger than magnitude 8. In anticipation of that event, several research groups are working hard to understand how the Alpine Fault is being loaded prior to its next rupture and how its geometry and physical characteristics may affect an earthquake’s propagation and the resulting ground shaking. Our focus is on determining the fault’s geometry and internal structure at scales much finer than can be studied using conventional seismometers, which are usually spaced tens of kilometres apart. Instead we used a standard telecommunications cable to reveal the fault’s internal detail. Our study shows the fault is not a single clean crack but rather a band of damaged rock about 200 metres wide. The Alpine Fault is a wide band of damaged rock, with narrower zones where it likely slipped. Author provided , CC BY-SA Within it, we found six much narrower zones of more intensely crushed and sheared rock. We call these “cores” and think the most prominent core is where the fault slipped during recent large earthquakes. This matters because an earthquake’s size depends mainly on how much of the fault breaks. Understanding the fault’s structure helps us work out how much could break at once, and how large the next big earthquake might be. Lighting up the Alpine Fault We send pulses of laser light down an optical fibre in a cable installed by telecommunications company Chorus near Haast. This turns the cable into a long line of sensitive earthquake sensors. We used a technique called distributed acoustic sensing ( DAS ). This records microscopic vibrations of the cable by measuring how each laser pulse is scattered by atomic-scale imperfections in the glass fibre. Our measurements show seismic waves produced by nearby small earthquakes travel along the fault as distinctive energy pulses known as fault zone guided waves. The propagation of these waves along a fault is similar to how light travels along an optical fibre. The fault zone guided waves we have recorded reveal the discrete cores, only about 10 metres wide, within the 200-metre zone of damaged rock. A fibre-optic cable near Haast recorded earthquake waves guided by the Alpine Fault, revealing several narrow fault cores within a wider zone of damaged rock. The circle size shows earthquake magnitude. Green circles mark earthquakes with clear guided waves, and orange circles mark those with less distinct guided waves. Voon Hui Lai , CC BY-SA Our observations suggest one of the cores extends continuously for about 180 kilometres along the Alpine Fault, from Martins Bay at least as far as Karangarua. While the fault bends and kinks at the surface, our new measurements imply that, deep underground, its main slip zone appears to be largely continuous. Whether slip occurs on a single smooth surface, as our observations suggest, or on separate, discontinuous fault structures likely influences the extent and direction of rupture, and hence the ground shaking it produces. Significantly, the most prominent core extends across a distinct change in the Alpine Fault’s geometry near Martyr River. There the dipping geometry characteristic of the fault along much of the West Coast alters to a steeper, almost vertical geometry extending towards Milford Sound. Earlier research suggests many past earthquakes have started or stopped near Martyr River. Determining which factors control the start and end of an earthquake along the Alpine Fault, including whether slip occurs on a single, continuous surface or jumps between separate faults, is crucial to understanding the likely extent of future ruptures. This in turn determines the earthquake’s overall magnitude and resulting ground shaking. Another recent study used grooves scratched onto a fault plane, known as “slickenlines”, to show the Alpine Fault ruptured from south to north in the last large earthquake in 1717. If a future Alpine Fault quake were to rupture in a south to north direction, it would cause higher-intensity shaking in the populated regions of Canterbury, Marlborough, Tasman and the northern West Coast. In contrast, a north to south rupture would propagate towards Fiordland, where fewer people live. The DAS measurements we made at Haast enable us to describe the fine-scale internal structure of the Alpine Fault at depths relevant to earthquake nucleation and propagation. Together with other studies, we are building a clearer picture of how different sections of the fault are connected in locations where large earthquakes appear to preferentially start or stop. Our observations will provide vital information for future models of rupture progression and the radiation of seismic energy that causes ground shaking. Understanding this will help New Zealand prepare for the hazard and the impacts of future Alpine Fault earthquakes. John Townend has received funding from the Catalyst and Marsden funds, both administered by the Royal Society Te Apārangi; the Natural Hazards Commission Toka Tū Ake; and the Ministry of Business, Innovation, and Employment. He serves as chair of the publications committee of the Seismological Society of America. Meghan S. Miller receives funding from the Australian Research Council and from National Collaborative Research Infrastructure Strategy (NCRIS) in her role as program director of AuScope Earth Imaging. Voon Hui Lai receives funding from Singapore Ministry of Education (MOE) AcRF Tier 3b project “Investigating Volcano and Earthquake Science and Technology (InVEST)”.

articles.content: New tariffs planned as Trump administration clamps down on ‘unfair trade practices’ Hannah Webster , senior economist at the think tank New Economics Foundation , also called for other measures. The price cap increase will be difficult news for households to bear, especially during the winter when our energy needs and bills are higher. The government’s current support measures don’t match the reality of rising costs and squeezed household finances. The £100 payment announced at the budget won’t cover the increase that’s coming, nor is it available to every household. According to NEF analysis, one million low-income households will miss out. Today’s price cap rise shows how exposed households remain to imported energy - the answer is to generate more at home. Biomethane, made from farms and food waste, is already flowing through our grid - enough to heat around a million homes - but NESO [National Energy System Operator] has just cut its outlook for biomethane because of policy uncertainty. Continue reading...

articles.content: A war correspondent interviewed 100 sources about the pop star, but what does the 4,500-word story reveal? If you are extremely online you will have known for a while that a big takedown was coming. An exposé of a well-known blond billionaire, a powerful figure that people are terrified to criticise, was in the works at a large publication. A former war correspondent had been assigned the story! A hundred sources had been interviewed! The reporting had taken a year! The truth would finally out! For everyone else, let me explain in plain English. On Monday Vanity Fair published an eagerly anticipated, 4,500-word piece, about Taylor Swift called The Mastermind. While it was labelled as “commentary”, it was framed as a deeply sourced piece written by May Jeong, a journalism professor at Princeton who has won awards for her reporting from Afghanistan. Continue reading...

articles.author: Ben Fisher in Istanbul
articles.content: Unai Emery wanted the winger but, like Harvey Elliott last season, he has been left out in the cold despite Villa’s attacking struggles It is three years this week since Alejandro Garnacho opened the scoring for Manchester United in a 3-3 draw at Galatasaray in the Champions League, on a typically boisterous night in Istanbul when Victor Lindelöf and Aaron Wan-Bissaka, now his teammates at Aston Villa, were also among the starters. At the time, Garnacho was a teenage star flourishing on the grandest of stages, a fixture in the United team and fresh from scoring an outrageous overhead kick at Goodison Park a few days earlier that would later clinch the Premier League’s goal-of-the-season award. He went on to score twice at Old Trafford on Boxing Day, in a 3-2 victory against Villa, and a couple of months later his double at home to West Ham was the catalyst for that iconic celebration photo of Garnacho, Kobbie Mainoo and Rasmus Højlund sitting on the advertising hoardings at the Stretford End, beaming smiles all round. All three were at the heart of United’s plans for a bright future, beacons of hope. At the end of that season, Garnacho signed off in style, he and Mainoo scoring against Manchester City at Wembley to win the FA Cup . Continue reading...

articles.content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Early in the second half of Tuesday night’s National League South match between Torquay United and Chesham, play was briefly suspended due to an ear-splitting din emitted over the Plainmoor public address system. “The game has stopped because the Torquay Tannoy system is making a loud noise that won’t stop,” posted Chesham on their Social Media Disgrace account. “I’m not kidding.” A sort of aural cross between an ocean liner’s foghorn and a party conference speech delivered by a senior member of the Reform party, it eventually stopped and play resumed with Torquay running out 2-1 winners. In this constantly changing world of global disruptions, uncertainties and risks, with social, political and economic disaffection seemingly on the rise everywhere, it’s genuinely heartening to know that some things never change . ‘Plus ça change, plus c’est la même chose’, as the late, great French writer Jean-Baptiste Alphonse Karr famously said, something that I’m sure Big Dunc is well aware of” – Noble Francis. May I be the 1,092nd correspondent to demand a review of the Letter o’ the Day award for Monday – and it be awarded to Declan Hackett for his letter foretelling the rescinding of the red card given to Lenny Yoro on Sunday? Given the precedent of awarding/revoking/re-awarding of the Afcon 2025 edition this would be entirely justified” – Peter Martin. This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. To get the full version, just visit this page and follow the instructions . Continue reading...

articles.author: Keith Stuart
articles.content: Rockstar’s latest blockbuster makes the everyday business of shopping, working out and taking care of a pet snake as compelling as its shootouts and car chases I knew I’d need many skills during the opening hours of Grand Theft Auto VI, but effective time management was not one of them. From playing the previous five titles in the series (and their many spin-offs), I understood I’d have to master Rockstar’s idiosyncratic approach to car handling. True enough, the vehicles do drive like airbeds tied on top of supermarket trolleys. I also knew I’d need to get to grips with the somewhat tricky aiming and shooting if I was to commit any sort of respectable crime spree. But for the first few hours of playing this staggeringly large and bewildering game, what concerned me most was lead character Jason’s personal routine. Each day, he needs to get up, choose an outfit, complete a workout, feed his pet snake Dolores, and perhaps do some DIY, so that when his girlfriend Lucia gets out of jail she’ll fall for him again – rather than fall through his apartment’s rotten staircase. Meanwhile, his drug-smuggling boss phones every five minutes with new parcels for Jason to pick up or drop off, and his pals Cal and Donnie get into all sorts of cocaine-related hijinks they expect Jason to extricate them from. There are also predatory neighbours to do favours for, and groceries to buy. I’ve seen so many people on social media posting about how they took several days off work to play this game, only to find themselves busier and more productive than ever. On his radio show last week, James O’Brien derided himself for completing, in Jason’s apartment, a simple DIY task that he’s put off for months in his own home. I know where he’s coming from. Continue reading...

articles.author: Andrew Beasley
articles.content: While referees tend to reach for red early in the season before easing off, players are under increasing pressure to keep pace in a frenetic environment Off! Off! Off! The past three Premier League games have featured a red card, each for a different reason. Brighton’s Costinha was sent off for two bookings at Hull, Leny Yoro collected a red card against Liverpool for denying a goalscoring opportunity ( though his suspension was overturned on appeal) and James Tarkowski saw red for serious foul play at Brentford. This season is shaping up to be an outlier in the VAR era of officiating in English football. The latest red cards took the Premier League total to 22 in 2026-27. The rate of 0.2 per game equates to 76 across the whole season, which would equal the Premier League record set in 2005-06. Refereeing has evolved in the past decade, though. The average across the seven completed campaigns since VAR was introduced is 0.12 per game, with a high of 0.15 in 2023-24. Continue reading...

articles.author: Alaina Demopoulos
articles.content: A generation known for loneliness is putting their own spin on a millennial-made tradition that requires socializing It’s a TikTok scene straight out of a stress dream: two men stand in their freshly cleaned apartment, explaining how all but one of the people they invited to Friendsgiving flaked out at the last minute. There is a can of whipped cream on the table and a 6lb ham in the oven. According to the video, posted by pop-culture podcaster Jackson Strike, those who ditched were either tired, or sick, or had a difficult day at work. More than 1.5 million people liked the video and many flooded to the comments section to express their disappointment at what they saw as an epidemic of antisocial behavior. “Everyone wants a village until they have to be a villager,” one user wrote. “Time to get new friends,” quipped another. Continue reading...

articles.content: Dario Russo’s debut feature is Brothers Grimm meets Yorgos Lanthimos, with a standout cast including Olivia Colman, Sam Neill and Emily Browning The vibe of writer-director Dario Russo’s delightfully peculiar feature debut is “messed-up fairytale”, pitched somewhere between the Brothers Grimm and Yorgos Lanthimos, with a distinctly Australian je ne sais quoi . I love how this film feels as though it was made in consultation with the animal world, taking place in a universe where animals can speak to humans – though that’s perhaps the least weird thing about it. articles.author: Martin Pegan
articles.content: One or perhaps more spots are up for grabs ahead of the summer series against New Zealand. We assess the leading batters’ chances of being picked in the XI Australia’s cricketers would be within their rights to be counting down the days until attention turns to the first Test of the home summer against New Zealand in Perth. As the sandpapergate scandal overshadows a pair of white-ball series against arch-rivals England, batters around the country have been pressing their claims for a place in Australia’s XI when the Chappell-Hadlee Trophy series begins on 9 December. A vacancy has already opened at the top of the order after selectors took the unusual step to confirm earlier this month that Marnus Labuschagne had been dropped from the squad for the four-Test series. The race to replace Australia’s No 3 – whether slotting straight into Labuschagne’s spot at first drop or as part of a batting order reshuffle – has become packed with Test discards and an emerging talent hoping to earn a debut. The door could open for more than one addition to the XI alongside presumed incumbents Travis Head, Matt Renshaw, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Josh Inglis and wicketkeeper Alex Carey, with worrying signs Australia’s ageing squad is starting to creak after three defeats in their past five Tests. Continue reading...

articles.author: Osasu Obayiuwana in Lagos
articles.content: After African football was dragged into needless disrepute the next step is to tackle two key areas of governance A journey of 310 days and three legal proceedings to confirm two things we know – that Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 to win the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and, most importantly, that the decision of a referee remains final and sacrosanct – has produced the longest, most comical and embarrassing Afcon final in the tournament’s 69-year history. As the Confederation of African Football (Caf) executive committee member Samir Sobha told the Guardian, the decision of the organisation’s appeals board in March to overturn Senegal’s victory and award the title to Morocco, prompting a legal charade ended by the court of arbitration for sport’s verdict on Tuesday , was a “big joke” that brought Caf and the Afcon into needless disrepute. Continue reading...

articles.author: Adrian Horton
articles.content: Writer-director Beth de Araújo witnessed a brutal sexual assault as a child and has turned her experience into one of the year’s most powerful movies The film-maker Beth de Araújo likens the personal experience that inspired Josephine, her disquieting second feature, to a slow-acting poison. Early one Saturday morning when she was eight years old, Araújo and her father were playing soccer in Golden Gate Park, near their home in San Francisco, when they heard a woman scream. Her father, a former Olympic runner for Brazil, told her to stay and bolted to help; Araújo, scared and alone, ran after him, and instead found the woman in a clearing, naked from the waist down. Araújo was too young to understand what had happened, but she knew something was wrong. So, too, does an eight-year-old Josephine, played by the remarkable newcomer Mason Reeves, in the one scene crafted exactly to Araújo’s memory: Josephine, confused and restless, observes as the woman tucks her hands under her legs to keep them from shaking. She is further confused when her father, Damien, played by the aspirationally everyman actor Channing Tatum, seems extra keen to return to their soccer game afterwards, one of many echoes of Araújo’s memory in this taut drama. In real life, Araújo’s father “put on a face, put on energy and made it seem fun,” she recalled. “And I was like: ‘This is so weird. Why is my dad being so extra fun right now?’” Continue reading...

articles.content: The pair, who met in 2010, are shown preparing for the Dublin race to raise awareness of Fogarty’s epidermolysis bullosa in Rachel Fleit’s considerate documentary The personal scenes in this film from Rachel Fleit have been carefully controlled and curated, the privacy of both parties being important, for different and understandable reasons. But it is an unexpectedly intimate, emotional piece of work, a big-hearted odd-couple story, which is perhaps slightly more complex than at first appears. Emma Fogarty is a smart, garrulous woman from Abbeyleix in County Laois in the Republic of Ireland who has EB: epidermolysis bullosa, a rare condition which means that her skin is permanently, agonisingly painful and requires a daily calvary of bandaging and re-bandaging. While getting an award at the People of the year event in 2010 for her campaigning work educating the public about this illness, Emma met and struck up a friendship with Colin Farrell, a supporter and patron of the EB charity Debra Ireland . Continue reading...

articles.content: The job of Mauricio Pochettino’s successor is to fine-tune a team on the up. That requires a bureaucrat rather than a figurehead First, let’s get the Pep Exception out of the way. Or perhaps we’d better call it the Guardiola Caveat. Regardless, the point is the same. If US Soccer can get Pep Guardiola to manage the United States men’s national team, it should. Because when you have the chance to employ the most successful and influential coach of his generation, the thinker who stands upstream of essentially every major tactical current of the last two decades, you just have to do it. But let us assume that US Soccer can’t appoint Guardiola, because he is only a few months into his post-Manchester City sabbatical and still busying himself defending his body of work . Because he has given no recent indication that he wants the job, even though he spent a previous break between managerial gigs living in New York City and was probably only being supportive of his newly-appointed colleague Mauricio Pochettino when he called the project “fascinating” two years ago. Also because he has only ever signed on to coach teams stacked with Ballon d’Or contenders, posing a Phil Jackson-type, bar-room question over whether he would still be exceptional in charge of unexceptional players. Continue reading...

articles.author: Yagnishsing Dawoor
articles.content: The Norwegian Nobel laureate’s sequel to Vaim explores what happens when a man is stripped of everything that tells him who he is Very strange things happen in Jon Fosse’s 2025 novel Vaim . A man meets a woman he secretly loved in his youth while running an errand in a nearby town. She asks him to take her away with him, to the place where they both grew up, on the boat he named after her. She wants to live with him, she tells him, even though she is married, and he has never admitted his feelings. This same man, in another section, has now died. The woman returns to her husband, and tells him he must get back with her, but he has to answer to the name she gave him when they lived together. He must also move into the home of the man she had left him for. “All was strange,” the husband admits, and decides those words should be on his tombstone. Indeed, all is – and remains – very strange to the reader: the powerlessness of these men before this woman they hardly seem to know; the randomness of the events in their lives; their spooky, dream-like surreality. But most of all: Fosse’s narrative choices that thwart easy rationalisation. Vaim Hotel is the second volume in the Nobel laureate’s loosely connected trilogy-in-progress set in the fictional Norwegian town of Vaim. Told in Fosse’s hypnotically recursive style, in a nimble translation by Damion Searls, it is ostensibly a tale of captivity that is only a touch less disorienting than its predecessor, thanks in part to the thematic correspondences it establishes. Beckettian in its relish for the absurd and the tediously mundane, this single-sentence novel opens with a man in his 50s who, for reasons he cannot quite explain, drives to Vaim, and decides to lodge at the empty Vaim Hotel, as yet unaware that he might never leave. Here, too, we have a mysterious female figure before whom male agency fails: Brita, owner of the hotel. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jack Seale
articles.content: In this adaptation of the sci-fi franchise Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer are on a quest to track down a group of replicants gone rogue. It’s a neon-filled world of beautiful doomsday visions Memory: the mother of the muses, and the heart of the Blade Runner franchise. Science fiction is forever asking what it means to be human and, in the future dystopia first painted by Ridley Scott’s 1982 movie, the answer is that we are what we remember: we are the experiences we preserve as a collection of short films inside our heads. In the original Blade Runner, Rachael (Sean Young) is devastated to learn that her childhood memories aren’t real, and she is therefore a robot “replicant”; in Denis Villeneuve’s sequel, Blade Runner 2049, K (Ryan Gosling) knows he’s a replicant but hopes his memories are a sign that he is something close to human. Blade Runner has always been relevant to the age of AI, in that its starting point is that enslaved robots have rebelled. But the new version, the story’s first expansion into television, is acutely topical in an era where we’re increasingly anxious about whether what we’re seeing – or reading – is the work of machines. Fifty years on from the events of the last movie, the replicants have won: “Blade runners” are now replicants hunting down disobedient humans rather than the other way around, and the capture and storage of human memories is illegal. As humanity dies, what it remembers has become valuable contraband. Continue reading...

articles.content: Four umpires discuss how they deal with players, why they avoid social media, how technology is changing cricket and why umpiring beats being a football referee By Wisden Cricket Monthly Last summer, sat in a quiet ground at the fag-end of a four-dayer, with a few souls still kicking around and a clutch of cameras streaming what was left of the day live on YouTube, it struck me again what a great, strange sanctuary this place is, out there on the edges of the modern world. articles.author: Andrew Downie
articles.content: A new book charts the complicated relationship between the two legends, starting on a sunny afternoon in Rio in 1979 Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, not long after the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to the finals of the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio. Reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. He collared the young man after Argentine Juniors played Huracán and then raced to the airport and put him on a plane with his father, his agent and a photographer. Continue reading...
